title: Lotus Sutra 4
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching is that even in our spiritual journey, we often don't realize who has been guiding us along the way. The Buddha shares a story from his past life about how he was taught the Lotus Sutra by his teacher Devadatta, who later became his nemesis. This teaches us to look beyond our ego and recognize the role that others have played in our spiritual growth, even if they may not be immediately apparent or pleasant to acknowledge. By understanding this dynamic, we can deepen our appreciation for the interconnectedness of all beings and cultivate a sense of humility and gratitude for the guidance we've received. This insight can help us navigate our own spiritual journeys with greater awareness and compassion.

sentences.text: Enter the cosmic realms here.
We have one more week on the Lotus Sutta after this one, and I think it will be no problem to get through all the parts that are important, or at least the parts that I think are important.
We left off last time on Chapter 11, where the stupa emerged hovering in the sky, and all these Buddhas appeared from everywhere, hovering around it.
And this stupa, even though it's not mentioned in the subsequent chapters, or at least for a while, you have to imagine it's hovering there this whole time.
It's just up there this whole time.
In the next chapter is the famous Devadatta Chapter, and this is a really important chapter.
The Buddha says:
*A long time ago, I sought the Lotus Sutra without ever flagging.
I was looking for it, and I couldn't find it.
And during those many kalpas, when I was looking for it, I constantly appeared as the ruler of a kingdom who made a vow to seek the unsurpassed Bodhi.*
So I was that king, the Buddha said, many lifetimes ago.
*And at the time that I was this king, there was a seer,* I guess like a religious sage, *who came to me and said, I have a great vehicle text called the Sutra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law.
If you will never disobey me, I will expound it for you.*
*And when I, that king, heard these words, I was very excited, I danced for joy, and I did.
I obeyed and served that seer for a thousand years, all for the sake of the law, of the Dharma, working diligently, acting as a provider, and seeing to it that the seer lacked for nothing.*
Then the amazing revelation comes: the king at that time was I myself, the Buddha.
And who do you think the seer was?
It was Devadatta.
Devadatta was the Buddha's teacher in this past life who gave him the Lotus Sutra.

*All because Devadatta was a good friend to me, I was able to become fully endowed with the six paramitas, with pity, compassion, joy and indifference,* the four immeasurables, loving-kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity, *with the 32 features, the 80 characteristics and so on and so on.
The fact that I have attained impartial and correct enlightenment and can save living beings on a broad scale is all due to Devadatta who was a good friend and taught me the Lotus Sutra.*
Now, maybe you're not impressed with this, we've seen a lot already.
What's the big deal?
Well, it is a big deal.
And the reason why it's such a big deal is because you've got to know who Devadatta is.
Devadatta is a very important person in the Buddha's life because Devadatta is the Buddha's nemesis.
Everybody has to have a nemesis, right?
So Devadatta was the Buddha's cousin who was apparently a very talented spiritual master who very early on decided that he wanted to overthrow the Buddha and sort of get the Sangha to be his Sangha.
